items.title: Three Companies, One Lesson: When AI Judges People, Trust Is the Business Model
items.author: Valery Meshkov
items.content:
I have started three companies, and in all of them, software makes some kind of judgment about people. At Pravoved.ru, the online legal marketplace I co-founded, it was about matching people with lawyers and answering their legal questions. At Jinn, an HR-tech platform, it was assessing employees and candidates for corporate clients. Now at Narvalus, which I co-founded in Miami, we are building an AI recruiting agent for U.S. hiring teams.

When I started each of them, I thought the main risk was technical. Will the model be accurate enough? It almost never turned out to be the problem. The problem was that people didn't believe the system, even when it was right. And that changed not only the product but how we sold it, priced it, and decided where to start.

At Pravoved, trust was the product.

When we launched Pravoved, legal help in Russia mostly meant going to an office, paying an unclear price, and hoping the lawyer was good. Nobody could compare. Our bet was that people would ask a question online if they could see several lawyers answer it and check their ratings from other clients.

That bet worked, but the interesting part came later. Most incoming questions were standard, the same consumer-law issues again and again. So we built an AI assistant trained on our lawyers' answers to handle them. Technically, it was fine. What made users accept it was that a real lawyer was always one click away and the reasoning was visible. When an answer came without context, people doubted it, even when it was correct.

The business lesson for me was simple. Automate what is standard, keep people for what is not, and never hide which is which. It also pushed us toward corporate clients. Companies wanted predictable, documented legal support, and over time B2B grew to about 65% of our revenue. Investors from AddVenture and Target Global backed that model, in part because trust was built into it and not added later.

At Jinn, clients didn't buy scores.

With Jinn, I moved into HR. The platform runs assessments, 360-degree feedback, and engagement surveys, and uses AI to turn that data into recommendations about people. We went from one corporate client to more than seventy in a few years.

For an HR director, the accuracy percentage of a model is not the real question. The real questions are "Can I explain this to the manager?" and "What do I tell the employee if they ask?" A score alone did not survive those questions. A score with clear reasons behind it did. So the explanation became the thing we really sold, and the score was more like a summary of it.

Narvalus: Same lesson, higher stakes.

Recruiting is where this matters most, because the AI influences who gets an interview and who doesn't. And in the U.S., the rules are getting stricter. New York City's Local Law 144 requires an independent bias audit, a published summary, and notice to candidates when automated employment decision tools are used. The EU AI Act puts AI used in recruitment in the high-risk category. And existing anti-discrimination law applies whether a person or a program made the decision.

So when we designed the Narvalus agent, we started from trust and worked back to the model. A few decisions came out of that.

The agent works from the job description, criterion by criterion. It turns the job description into concrete requirements and checks each candidate against each one, with a short reason for every match or gap. The recruiter can see exactly why someone is near the top, without writing Boolean search strings.

It flags questions; it doesn't reject. If two jobs on a resume overlap in time, or a career path is unusual, the agent marks it as something to ask in the interview. People make every hiring decision. This was not a hard choice for me after Pravoved: the unusual cases are exactly where a human is worth the most.

Scoring and auditing are kept apart. The scoring step is designed never to receive age, photos, gender, or other protected attributes. But just removing fields doesn't remove every proxy; a graduation year can still hint at age. So we are building the audit side separately: where candidates choose to share demographic data, it is stored apart from scoring and used only to report selection rates for bias audits. If you skip that part, you can't actually prove the first part works.

How trust shaped the business, not just the product.

This is the part I think founders underestimate. Explainability is shaping our go-to-market plan as much as our architecture.

First, the starting market. We chose to begin in Miami with staffing agencies and small and mid-sized employers. They have a lot of applicants and small teams, often without a dedicated sourcer or in-house counsel. A big company can afford to check a vendor's claims itself. A ten-person agency can't, so a tool that explains itself is worth more to them, and they can decide quickly.

Second, pricing. We plan a simple per-seat subscription with a free trial on real open roles. If the value is that recruiters trust the shortlist, the fastest way to prove it is to let them try it on their own vacancies, not to show a demo.

Third, the enterprise tier. Bias-audit reporting and documentation will go into the higher plan. Larger employers carry more legal exposure, and for them compliance is not a nice extra. It decides whether the deal moves forward at all.

What I would tell other founders.

If your product judges people in some way, for jobs, loans, housing, or legal help, build for the most skeptical person who will read the output: a regulator, a lawyer, or the person being judged. If the explanation doesn't hold up for them, the feature is not finished. And design your business around that skeptic too, because they are often the one who signs off on the purchase.

At Pravoved, the AI never replaced lawyers. It took the routine questions so lawyers had more time for the hard ones. I believe recruiting will go the same way. In a year or two, we will see if I was right.

Valery Meshkov is a serial technology entrepreneur. He co-founded Pravoved.ru, an online legal marketplace backed by AddVenture and Target Global, founded the HR-tech platform Jinn, and is a co-founder of Narvalus, an early-stage company developing an AI recruiting agent for U.S. hiring teams.

items.title: When a Small Team Should (and Shouldn't) Adopt Kubernetes
items.author: Alana stefan
items.content:
Kubernetes has become the default answer to almost every infrastructure question. Read a few conference talks or job postings, and it can feel like running anything else is a mistake. But Kubernetes was built at Google scale, for problems most small teams do not have yet.

For a team of three to fifteen engineers, adopting Kubernetes too early can cost months of productivity. Adopting it too late can leave you stuck with fragile deployments. This post gives you a practical way to decide.

What Kubernetes Actually Gives You

Kubernetes is a container orchestrator. It schedules containers across machines, restarts them when they fail, rolls out new versions gradually, scales them up and down, and gives them a consistent way to find each other on the network.

Those are real benefits. But each one comes with something you have to learn, configure, and maintain: networking, ingress, storage, RBAC, secrets, upgrades, monitoring, and cost control. The platform does not remove operational work. It moves the work to a different layer.

When a Small Team Should Adopt Kubernetes

  • You run many services that need to scale independently

If you have a dozen or more services and each has different traffic patterns, orchestration starts to pay off. Scaling one busy service without touching the others is exactly what Kubernetes does well.

  • You need frequent, safe, zero-downtime releases  

Rolling updates, readiness probes, and easy rollbacks are built in. If you ship several times a day and downtime directly costs revenue, this is a strong reason to adopt.  

  •  You already have containerization and CI/CD habits

Teams that already build container images, run automated tests, and deploy through a pipeline can adopt Kubernetes far more smoothly.

The platform fits into a workflow that already exists. 

  • You need portability across clouds or environments

If customers require deployment in different clouds, or you want to avoid deep lock-in to a single provider's compute service, Kubernetes gives you a common layer.

  • Someone on the team genuinely owns it

This is the most overlooked condition. Kubernetes needs at least one person who understands it deeply, or a partner who does. Without an owner, small problems become long outages.

When a Small Team Should Not Adopt Kubernetes

  •  You have one application, or a handful

A monolith or a few services rarely need orchestration. A well-configured virtual machine, or a managed platform, is simpler and cheaper.

  • Your traffic is steady and predictable

If load barely changes, autoscaling gives you very little. You would be paying a complexity cost for a feature you do not use

  • Nobody on the team has operated it before

Learning Kubernetes in production, during an incident, is painful. A steep learning curve combined with a small team is the most common cause of failed adoptions.

  • You are still finding product-market fit

Early-stage teams should spend their time on the product. Infrastructure that lets you ship the next feature faster is better than infrastructure that is impressive.   

  • You are adopting it because it looks good on a CV or a pitch deck

Trend-driven adoption is expensive. If you cannot name the specific problem Kubernetes solves for you, you probably do not need it yet.

Simpler Options to Consider First

Skipping Kubernetes does not mean skipping good practice. Several options give you most of the benefits with much less overhead:

  • Managed container services such as AWS ECS with Fargate, Google Cloud Run or Azure Container Apps. You run containers without managing a cluster.
  • Platform-as-a-service options such as Heroku, Render or Elastic Beanstalk for straightforward web applications.
  • Docker Compose on a single server for small internal tools or early products, paired with good backups and monitoring.
  • Managed Kubernetes (EKS, GKE, AKS) if you do decide to adopt. It removes control-plane maintenance, which is the hardest part to run yourself.

Many teams start with one of these and move to Kubernetes later. Because the workloads are already containerized, that migration is far easier than starting from scratch.

A Quick Decision Checklist

Ask yourself these questions honestly:

  1. Do we run more than roughly ten services, or expect to within a year?
  2. Do different services need to scale independently?
  3. Do we deploy often, and does downtime hurt us financially?
  4. Is our application already containerized, with a working CI/CD pipeline?
  5. Do we have at least one person who can own the cluster, or a reliable partner?
  6. Can we budget time for upgrades, security patching, and monitoring?

If you answered yes to most of these, Kubernetes is probably a good fit. If you answered no to most, a simpler platform will likely serve you better for now.

If You Do Adopt It, Start Small

  • Use a managed control plane rather than running your own.
  • Begin with one non-critical workload and learn from it.
  • Set resource requests and limits from day one to avoid noisy-neighbour problems and surprise bills.
  • Invest early in monitoring and alerting, since a cluster you cannot observe is a cluster you cannot trust.
  • Keep configuration in version control and automate deployments with CI/CD.
  • Plan regular upgrades. Kubernetes versions leave support quickly.

Kubernetes is a powerful tool, not a milestone. The right question is not "Are we big enough for Kubernetes?" but "Do we have problems that Kubernetes solves better than anything simpler?"

For many small teams, the honest answer is not yet, and that is a perfectly good engineering decision. Choose the simplest platform that meets your reliability needs today, keep your workloads containerized, and move to Kubernetes when the pain of not having it clearly outweighs the cost of running it.

items.title: Modernizing Enterprise Storage: How Automation and AI Are Changing Infrastructure Engineering
items.author: Sanya Kapoor
items.content:
Enterprise storage infrastructure rarely receives attention until something goes wrong. Yet behind business applications, databases, analytics platforms, and digital services are complex systems responsible for storing, protecting, and making data available. As organizations accumulate larger volumes of information, modernizing these environments becomes an engineering challenge involving architecture, performance, connectivity, validation, and operational risk.

For Nikhil Kumar Aedla, a Principal Data Storage Engineer, enterprise storage modernization involves more than transferring information between platforms. His work supporting a multi-petabyte storage migration brings together infrastructure planning, storage area network (SAN) connectivity, automation, validation, and AI-assisted operational analysis. The approach reflects a broader question facing infrastructure teams: how can organizations modernize large storage environments while maintaining control over the systems and data that depend on them?

Why Enterprise Storage Modernization Is More Than a Data Transfer

Large enterprise storage environments often contain infrastructure introduced over many years. Different generations of storage platforms, interconnected hosts, application dependencies, and established operational procedures can make modernization difficult to coordinate.

Moving data from an older storage environment to a newer platform requires an understanding of how applications access storage, how SAN paths are configured, how capacity is allocated, and how performance requirements influence migration sequencing. Maintenance windows, compatibility, rollback planning, and business continuity also need to be considered.

At multi-petabyte scale, treating the migration as a single transfer overlooks the relationships between infrastructure components. Each stage needs appropriate preparation and validation so that issues can be identified and addressed before the next stage proceeds.

Nikhil’s experience supporting enterprise storage modernization reflects this interconnected nature of the work. Storage architecture, host dependencies, migration planning, and operational coordination need to be considered together rather than managed as isolated technical activities.

Building a Structured Migration Strategy

A phased migration approach provides a way to organize complex infrastructure changes into manageable stages. Instead of moving an entire environment as one operation, engineers can plan migration waves around application priorities, infrastructure dependencies, maintenance windows, and performance requirements.

Preparation begins with understanding the existing environment. Capacity, SAN connectivity, host access, application relationships, and target-platform requirements all influence the migration sequence. Engineers must also establish how each stage will be validated and what procedures will apply if the expected conditions are not met.

Nikhil’s work has involved pre-migration readiness checks, dependency reviews, migration sequencing, and coordination across technical teams. These activities help define the operational requirements for each phase and establish what needs to be checked before and after data movement.

A phased approach also creates opportunities to review earlier migration activities before proceeding with subsequent stages. This makes documentation, consistent procedures, and clear status tracking important parts of the overall engineering process.

Using Automation to Make Infrastructure Work Repeatable

Large storage environments generate substantial amounts of routine administrative work. Engineers may need to collect configuration information, check connectivity, validate capacity, compare source and target settings, track migration progress, and prepare operational reports.

When these activities depend entirely on manual execution, maintaining consistency across repeated migration tasks can become difficult. Automation provides a way to standardize predictable procedures and make their execution easier to track.

In Nikhil’s storage modernization work, Ansible, Python, and PowerShell were used to support repeatable infrastructure operations. Ansible can orchestrate defined tasks, while Python and PowerShell can support scripting, data handling, validation, reporting, and platform-specific administrative activities.

The objective is not to automate every engineering decision. Instead, repeatable procedures can be automated while engineers retain responsibility for architecture choices, exception handling, production approvals, and risk assessment.

This distinction matters because infrastructure automation operates within environments where an incorrect change can affect multiple dependent systems. A reliable workflow needs to make its actions, validation steps, and failure conditions understandable to the people responsible for operating it.

Where AI-Assisted Operations Fit Into Storage Engineering

Automation and artificial intelligence address related but different problems. Automation executes predefined procedures, while AI-assisted analysis can help engineers interpret information produced by complex infrastructure environments.

Storage systems generate logs, alerts, configuration outputs, migration status records, and performance information. When an issue involves multiple infrastructure layers, engineers may need to examine information from storage platforms, SAN connections, hosts, and applications before determining what happened.

Nikhil’s work incorporates AI-assisted tools as a support layer for reviewing operational information. These tools can help summarize logs, group related alerts, compare expected and observed conditions, and highlight configuration differences that warrant investigation.

AI can also help organize source and target information into a clearer view during migration validation. Rather than requiring engineers to begin with large collections of raw operational data, an AI-assisted workflow can help direct attention toward specific exceptions and questions.

The output, however, is not the same as a verified diagnosis. An identified pattern or summarized alert needs to be checked against the underlying evidence and the technical context of the environment.

Enterprise infrastructure requires clear accountability for decisions that affect production systems. An AI-generated recommendation may be useful, but it should not automatically become an approved infrastructure change.

In storage modernization, this distinction is especially important when decisions involve data integrity, application availability, connectivity, or recovery procedures. A summary of operational logs can help an engineer investigate an issue, but it cannot independently establish that a proposed action is appropriate for every dependent system.

The operating approach described in Nikhil’s work keeps architecture decisions, production changes, approvals, exception handling, and risk acceptance under engineering control. AI assists with organizing information and narrowing the scope of investigation, while engineers verify the evidence and decide what to do next.

This division of responsibilities allows AI to support operational analysis without bypassing established change-management and validation procedures. It also provides a practical framework for introducing AI into infrastructure environments where traceability and accountability remain essential.

Validation and Monitoring Before and After Migration

Migration validation is not a single check performed at the end of a project. It is an ongoing activity that helps establish whether the source environment is ready for a change and whether the target environment meets the expected requirements afterward.

Pre-migration checks can cover capacity, configuration, host dependencies, and connectivity. During execution, monitoring can help engineers identify unexpected conditions and review migration progress. After data movement, validation can examine storage configuration, accessibility, connectivity, and relevant operational conditions.

Nikhil’s approach combines standardized checks with monitoring and AI-assisted review. AI can help organize status information and identify exceptions for closer examination, but it does not replace technical validation.

This is particularly relevant when a problem can originate at different infrastructure layers. An apparent storage issue may involve SAN connectivity, host access, application behavior, or an automation workflow. Collecting repeatable technical information and correlating events can help engineers investigate the issue within the correct context.

Troubleshooting Across Connected Infrastructure Layers

Troubleshooting in enterprise storage environments often requires more than examining a single device or log. A problem may involve several interconnected components, and the available information may be distributed across different systems.

Automation can help collect consistent technical data, while AI-assisted analysis can summarize logs and identify relationships between events. Engineers can then use this information to investigate possible causes, assess operational risk, and determine the appropriate response.

The distinction between identifying a possible cause and confirming it is important. AI-generated summaries can guide investigation, but conclusions still require technical verification. The system context, recent changes, dependency relationships, and observed behavior all matter when determining whether an explanation fits the evidence.

For infrastructure teams, this makes AI most useful when it supports a disciplined troubleshooting process rather than operating as an independent decision-maker.

Applying the Approach Beyond Storage Migration

The principles involved in large-scale storage modernization also apply to other infrastructure programs. Data-center consolidation, SAN modernization, storage refreshes, backup changes, disaster-recovery planning, and hybrid-cloud adoption all require coordination across interconnected systems.

These activities share several operational concerns, including dependency mapping, configuration consistency, validation, monitoring, change control, and recovery planning. Automation can help standardize repeatable procedures, while AI-assisted analysis can help engineers interpret the growing volume of information generated by infrastructure systems.

The appropriate use of these technologies depends on the environment and the task. A workflow that is suitable for summarizing operational logs may not be appropriate for automatically changing production configurations. Defining the boundary between assistance and execution is therefore an important part of infrastructure design.

Practical Considerations for Infrastructure Teams

Organizations planning storage modernization can begin by standardizing the procedures they already understand. Automation is easier to evaluate when the underlying process, expected inputs, validation requirements, and failure conditions are clearly defined.

Validation should be built into migration workflows rather than postponed until the final stage. Teams also need a clear way to track completed work, outstanding tasks, exceptions, and the technical evidence required before a migration phase can be closed.

AI-assisted analysis can then be introduced where it addresses a specific information-management problem, such as reviewing large log collections, summarizing status information, or correlating related events. Its output should remain subject to appropriate technical review, especially when recommendations could affect production availability, data integrity, security, or recovery.

Keeping workflows understandable is equally important. Engineers should be able to determine what an automated process did, why a validation failed, what changed, and who is responsible for the next decision.

The Future of AI-Assisted Infrastructure Engineering

Enterprise infrastructure is becoming increasingly interconnected, and the volume of operational information that engineers must interpret continues to make effective monitoring and analysis important. AI-assisted tools offer one way to organize this information, identify patterns, and support investigation across complex environments.

Nikhil Kumar Aedla’s work in enterprise storage modernization illustrates how these capabilities can be considered alongside established engineering practices. His approach combines storage architecture, SAN knowledge, phased migration planning, automation, validation, and AI-assisted operational analysis, while retaining human control over critical decisions.

The broader lesson is that infrastructure modernization is not simply a matter of adopting a new storage platform or introducing an AI tool. It requires a coordinated operating model in which technical fundamentals, repeatable processes, verification, and accountability work together.

As organizations continue to modernize their data environments, the practical role of AI will depend on how effectively it supports engineers in understanding complex systems and making informed decisions. In enterprise storage, the goal is not to replace engineering judgment, but to give it a clearer and more organized foundation.

items.title: What the Founders Who Dared to Start Actually Have in Common
items.author: Cedric
items.content:
Every founder story looks inevitable in hindsight. The garage, the first customer, the pivot that changed everything. But if you strip away the mythology, the founders who make it past the early years tend to share a handful of unglamorous habits. None of them are about being fearless. Most of them are about reducing the cost of being wrong.

This piece looks at what the data says about starting a company, and what the people who dared to start did differently.

The odds are real, but they are not the whole story.

Read that again: roughly half of new businesses do not reach their fifth birthday. That is not a reason to stay put. It is a reason to design your first years around survival, not around a perfect launch.

The founders who last usually treat those statistics as a design constraint. They ask a simple question early: what has to be true for us to still be here in year three?

Habit 1: They start from a gap, not from an idea.

Ideas are cheap. Gaps are expensive, because someone is already feeling the pain. The founders who build durable companies tend to start from a problem they have seen up close: in a previous job, in their neighborhood, in their own daily frustrations.

A practical test: can you name ten people who have this problem today, and would three of them pay to make it go away? If not, you have a hypothesis, not a business. That is fine, as long as you treat it as one.

Habit 2: They keep the first version small and cheap.

Survivors rarely bet everything on version one. They launch something narrow, charge for it early, and use real customer behavior to decide what to build next.

This is less about frugality and more about learning speed. Every month of runway you save is a month you can spend being wrong in useful ways. A smaller first version also makes it easier to admit when something is not working, because you have not sunk two years into it.

Habit 3: They do not romanticize failure.

The lesson is not "never fail." It is that failure only teaches you something if you deliberately extract the lesson. Founders who improve between ventures write down what went wrong, test those assumptions in the next project, and change their behavior instead of just their branding.

Habit 4: They borrow experience through mentors and networks.

Nobody builds alone, and the numbers back this up. A SCORE survey on small businesses found that mentored businesses were 12% more likely to remain in business after one year than the national average, and that business growth rose with the number of mentoring sessions.

A good mentor will not hand you a playbook. What they offer is pattern recognition: the ability to say "I have seen this go wrong before" while there is still time to change course. Peer networks do something similar. Talking to founders who are six months ahead of you is often more useful than reading another framework.

Habit 5: They study other people's journeys, critically.

Founder stories are useful when you read them as case studies rather than as motivation. The interesting parts are rarely the big wins. They are the boring decisions: the first hire, the pricing change, the market they chose not to enter.

If you want a starting point, French-speaking readers can browse a collection of entrepreneur journeys and success stories on henrypanky.com, which focuses on the courage to start, spotting market gaps, and learning from setbacks. Whatever you read, ask the same questions each time: what constraint did they face, what did they try first, and what would I have done differently?

Habit 6: They tell a clear story early.

Marketing is not something you bolt on after the product is ready. The founders who gain traction early can explain in one sentence who they help and why it matters. That sentence shapes the product, the pricing, and the first hires.

Clarity also makes you easier to help. Mentors, investors, and early customers can only point you to the right people if they understand exactly what you are doing.

A short checklist before you leap.

  • Can you describe the problem without mentioning your solution?
  • Have you talked to at least ten people who have that problem?
  • What is the smallest version you could charge for within 90 days?
  • How long can you survive if revenue takes twice as long as planned?
  • Who are two people you can call when you get stuck?
  • What would make you stop, and have you written it down?

Daring to start is not about ignoring the odds. It is about respecting them enough to build a company that can survive its own mistakes. The founders who make it are rarely the boldest people in the room. They are the ones who learn fastest, ask for help early, and keep their bets small until the market tells them to go big.

items.title: Why Your Rag Assistant Is Giving an Incorrect Answer Even Though It Found the Correct Document
items.author: Anil Reddy Putlacheru
items.content:
A developer queries an internal AI assistant. The assistant looks up the documentation, finds a relevant troubleshooting document, and provides an answer.

You get an incorrect answer.

This can seem like a problem with retrieval. Maybe the embedding model didn't find the correct document, or the index needs rebuilding.

But when you look at the retrieved documents, the correct document is already there.

This means you're potentially dealing with a reliability issue. The RAG system has found the relevant information, but it isn't giving you a reliable answer. Improving the search alone won't necessarily fix it.

The issue can occur after retrieval, when the application decides which information to trust, what it means, and whether there's enough evidence to answer the question.

You have multiple stages in a RAG system.

A RAG system has several stages.

The application takes in a question, finds relevant information from documents, and passes it to a language model to generate an answer based on the context provided.

Every part of this process can affect the outcome.

Say you have an internal troubleshooting assistant with documentation for three environments: Development, Staging, and Production.

A user asks what to do when their tests fail in Staging.

The search returns a troubleshooting document with the correct information for fixing issues in Staging. It also returns a runbook with similar instructions for Production.

Both documents are relevant to the general topic, but only one applies to the user's situation.

If the assistant combines them, the answer may contain technically correct information but give the wrong advice.

The issue here isn't necessarily with the search engine. It's with the application not maintaining enough context to know which information to use.

Irrelevant documents can be returned.

Vector searches are designed to return semantically relevant information.

However, they won't necessarily return the most up-to-date, authoritative, or environment-specific information.

Say you have three documents in your knowledge base. All describe how to restart a service.

One is an up-to-date runbook. Another is an old troubleshooting note, and the third is an incident report.

A similarity search may return all three because they discuss the same service and symptoms.

The assistant then needs to decide which document should be treated as the source of truth.

For a well-designed RAG system, you'll need metadata such as environment, system, version, publication date, and document type.

This metadata should be used during retrieval wherever possible to narrow the results to information that applies to the user's request.

If someone asks about Staging, we wouldn't want to recommend Production instructions just because the error messages are similar.

This can't always be solved by writing a more persuasive prompt. Some restrictions need to be enforced in the retrieval and application layers.

Chunking is another common reason for misleading answers.

Long documents are often broken into smaller chunks. This makes them easier to embed and search, but important conditions can become separated from the instructions they apply to.

Say you have a runbook containing this instruction:

Restart the worker if the queue is stuck for more than 10 minutes.

Later in the document, it says this should only be done in a non-production environment and only after confirming that no jobs are running.

If the retrieved chunk doesn't include those conditions, the model may recommend an action that isn't appropriate.

The wording in the chunk may be correct, but the information is incomplete.

Teams should test whether important conditions are preserved throughout document processing and retrieval.

For procedural documents, keeping headings, warnings, prerequisites and related steps together may be more useful than creating equal-sized chunks.

Where possible, chunk boundaries should follow the structure of the original document.

Say someone asks whether their integration tests are failing because of a recent deployment.

The assistant finds a deployment note and a few troubleshooting documents. None of them include the actual test execution logs.

The model may produce a plausible explanation based on similar issues, but there isn't enough evidence to confirm the cause.

A reliable assistant should distinguish between what is known and what remains uncertain.

The deployment documentation describes a failure pattern similar to the issue you're facing. However, without the execution logs, I couldn't confirm the cause.

This answer is less certain, but it's more useful.

It tells the user what information is missing and what to investigate next.

RAG systems should be tested on whether they recognise when there isn't enough evidence to provide a reliable answer.

Adding citations can make generated answers more transparent.

However, citations aren't useful if the referenced passages don't support the claims.

The assistant may cite a document discussing the correct service even though that document doesn't support its conclusion.

For example, a troubleshooting document may mention a timeout as one possible symptom.

The assistant might cite that document and confidently state that the timeout was caused by a recent deployment.

The citation looks legitimate, but it doesn't establish the cause.

Your evaluation should check the relationship between each claim and its cited passage.

In practice, you'll want to know whether the source supports the claim, whether it applies to the requested environment, and whether the assistant ignored contradictory evidence.

The presence of citations and the correctness of those citations should be measured separately.

Know where your issue is.

If your RAG assistant provides incorrect answers, you'll want to identify where the problem occurs.

This can be difficult if you're only testing the final response.

A useful approach is to break the evaluation into three areas:

  • Did the search return the correct documents needed to answer the question?
  • Were the documents current, applicable, and appropriate for the user's request?
  • Was the final answer supported by the retrieved evidence?

Say you have a test question with a known answer and a verified supporting source.

If the source never appears in the search results, retrieval needs investigation.

If the source appears but gets ignored during context selection, the issue is in the intermediate processing.

If the source reaches the model but the answer contradicts it, the problem is with answer generation or how the model uses the evidence.

Each of these issues requires a different solution.

Increasing the number of retrieved chunks may help when important documents are missing, but it can make other problems worse by introducing more irrelevant information.

Create test scenarios that show the limits of your RAG.

Your RAG evaluation should include scenarios that test the limits of the system.

Add questions involving outdated information, conflicting sources, and environment-specific conditions.

Include questions where no reliable source is available to support an answer.

Also add scenarios that check access controls. Just because a document is relevant doesn't mean the person asking the question is authorised to access it.

These tests help you understand whether the assistant can operate reliably in an enterprise environment.

Sometimes the correct response won't be a detailed explanation.

It may be to highlight conflicting information, ask for clarification, or explain that there isn't enough evidence to answer.

Say you have 100 test questions relating to troubleshooting procedures.

For each question, an engineer identifies the documents expected to be retrieved and the acceptable answer.

You then record whether the relevant evidence was found, whether the response used the correct sources, and whether its claims were supported.

You might find that most questions retrieve the correct documents, but the generated answers are not consistently grounded in those documents.

That would suggest improving vector search alone won't fix the main problem.

Instead, you could investigate context selection, source prioritization, and how the assistant handles conflicting information.

The 100 questions are only an illustrative example. In a real evaluation, you should report the actual results, how the dataset was built, and the criteria used to judge the answers.

Before releasing a RAG assistant to a wider audience, I'd want answers to a few questions:

  • Can the application filter documents by environment and user access?
  • Does it identify outdated information?
  • Are warnings and prerequisites preserved during retrieval?
  • Can it explain when there isn't enough evidence?
  • Do the citations actually support the claims?
  • Can engineers inspect the retrieved passages and identify where an incorrect answer originated?

These are practical checks that help determine whether a proof of concept can become a system that engineers can investigate, maintain, and rely on.

RAG can improve an AI assistant by connecting it to external information.

However, that information won't automatically be accurate, up-to-date, or appropriate for every question.

Your system may retrieve the correct document but still provide an incorrect answer because of missing conditions, conflicting sources, or unsupported claims.

That's why you need good document quality, appropriate retrieval filters, reliable context handling, and checks that verify whether the generated answer is supported by the evidence.

The goal isn't simply to retrieve more information.

It's to use the right information for the right question and recognise when there isn't enough evidence to give a reliable answer.

items.title: 5 Realistic Things that Could Happen to Privacy Coins in the Future
items.author: Obyte
items.content:
The privacy coin global landscape is getting… curious. While several authorities are all around trying to ban these assets, average users (and even institutions) don’t seem to really mind. Their prices have been soaring in the last year, as privacy becomes more valuable than ever before. And more than privacy, just the privacy coins’ own brands, considering some facts we’ll see ahead.

According to , the whole market capitalization of privacy tokens surpasses $85.4 billion, with Monero (XMR), Zcash (ZEC), and Dash (DASH) at the top of the ranking. They’re not alone, though. At least 277 additional privacy-related coins are listed there as well.

Their features vary, but most of them offer some kind of anonymous-enhancing mechanism for crypto transactions. This allows for the execution of private payments, donations, sensitive business transactions, protection of vulnerable parties, and financial activity where users prefer less public exposure.

Of course, authorities are likely only hearing about “money laundering” or some type of criminal activity, and that’s what begs the question: What could really happen to privacy coins in the future? We’ll try to answer that.

1. They’ll be More Regulated Than Ever

Well, this is already happening. was the first one to “ban” privacy coins in 2018, followed by other countries and regions in the years that came after. They include , (UAE), , , and as the last one, in 2026. The European Union (EU) in 2027, too. That’s 27 more countries blacklisting anonymous-enhancing tokens, alleging criminal concerns. However, it’s important to note what this “ban” really means in most cases. People can still own and use these tokens through self-custody wallets, but they won’t find them listed on regulated platforms and exchanges like Binance, Kraken, or OKX. These brands already delisted them, indeed, to comply with Anti-Money Laundering (AML) rules —where it’s usual to share explicit information about clients and transactions.

So, basically, more and more countries are forbidding crypto exchanges and custodians from listing . At this rate, it will be very difficult in the future to find regulated platforms where this type of cryptocurrency can be traded. Although at the very least, we still have decentralized exchanges.

2. Privacy Tech Will Go Beyond Coins

The privacy mechanisms behind privacy coins can be used for much more than anonymous payments, and these use cases could expand even further in the future. Zero-knowledge proofs, ring signatures, and CoinJoin are common techniques expanding beyond their original ecosystems, for instance. The first one is a cryptographic method for proving something is true without revealing the underlying information.

Ring signatures let someone sign on behalf of a group without revealing their identity. Meanwhile, CoinJoin is a transaction process that combines multiple users’ crypto transactions, making them harder to trace individually. Zcash, Monero, and Dash use these technologies, but they aren’t the only ones lately. Digital ID is a field receiving special attention. With zero-knowledge proofs, anyone can prove facts such as “I am over 18,” “I am a citizen,” or “I hold a valid credential” without revealing the underlying ID data. is one real example, and is doing the same to verify facts from government-issued credentials.

At the same time, can be used for anonymous e-voting, whistleblowing, e-bidding, and e-lotteries; and can offer a layer of privacy to public chains like Bitcoin or Ethereum. In the future, it won’t be unusual to find more and more of these technologies protecting the privacy of users who have never even thought about using them—and who may not even be fully aware that they’re using them.

3. There Will Be Greater Institutional Adoption

This is where brands start to matter more than just privacy. The reality seems to be that some investors want privacy coins… without the privacy part. Sometimes, without the “coin” part, too. Case in point, we already have the first Exchange-Traded Fund () for a private cryptocurrency (Zcash), launched by Grayscale in 2025. And not just that: ZEC's price has grown so much in the last year (by over 1,000%) that now share splits for investors to afford fractions of its ZEC fund. doesn’t end there, though. New market players, like (NIGHT) and (CC), are offering privacy-related products specifically designed for institutions. Midnight has programmable privacy, which means developers can select what specific data within their Dapp stays private, and what will be public —with compliance processes in mind. Canton has something similar, revealing transaction data only to authorized parties.

After all, privacy could have practical value for institutions. Companies may want to protect payment details, treasury movements, or business relationships from public network observers. The future here seems to be about investments, but also about private commercial operations while staying compliant.

Speaking of compliance, privacy and regulation are often presented as opposing forces, but future systems could make the relationship more nuanced. Selective disclosure is one possible bridge —as Midnight and Canton are proving. So, instead of exposing an entire financial history, a user could provide specific information to an authorized party when needed.

can also use cryptographic proofs to establish that certain conditions have been met without revealing unrelated information. Monero already has mechanisms that allow users to share certain transaction information through , although these don’t turn the network into a transparent chain. Future privacy systems could build on similar ideas. A financial service might need to establish that a transaction satisfies a particular rule, while the customer retains privacy over other details. Whether regulators accept particular implementations will depend on the jurisdiction and the rules involved. Still, the technology creates room for a model where privacy doesn’t automatically mean the absence of accountability.

Authorities worldwide would very much like to be able to track privacy coins, and that's a fact. In 2020, the US Internal Revenue Service (IRS) worth up to $625,000 each to Chainalysis and Integra FEC for developing cryptocurrency tracing tools targeting Monero, for instance. It didn't work, but privacy developers haven't sat idly by.

Even before that, in 2017, a study identified patterns that could help link some Monero transactions to their real inputs. the concerns and discussed changes to its mixin-selection method, which helps obscure the actual transaction inputs. In the same way, Zcash has been updating and improving its cryptographic structure .

Meanwhile, other coins are developing their own systems. Firo, for example, released its new privacy protocol in 2024. It's designed to conceal senders, recipients, amounts, and transaction links, and has independent cryptographic and code audits. Looking ahead, privacy coins may keep refining their cryptography, testing new defenses, and patching weaknesses as researchers uncover them. The challenge will be maintaining strong privacy as analytical techniques evolve.

Blackbytes & Optional Privacy

Far from the realm that global regulators can reach (e.g., crypto exchanges and custodians), we have another privacy option in Obyte: (GBB). This is a privacy coin designed to never touch a centralized exchange, and instead be traded directly peer-to-peer through the Obyte wallet and conditional payments.

In general, is a public network, but by using GBB you can hide all data about senders, recipients, and their transactions. This information only exists on your own device. Some features for regulated environments are also available, including a co-sign by the issuer (i.e., a financial institution) and attested tokens to verify the identity of authorized users. This way, without losing its public nature, Obyte also offers optional privacy for individuals and institutions.

An official extension for Anthropic’s Claude model was backdoored and threatened as many as 5,000 developers' machines, multiple sources reported Friday. Anthropic so far has yet to warn customers of the incident.

The compromised package was a VS Code extension available in the marketplace of Cursor, a maker of AI-assisted developer tools, the company said Friday. The malicious version, 2.1.313, subsequently affected “at most 5,000 users,” presumably when they either downloaded it or their systems automatically fetched and installed it. Anthropic pushed version 2.1.314 several hours after the previous version became available on Cursor, according to independent researcher Kevin Beaumont. Both Beaumont and the CTO and co-founder of security firm Phorian said that version 2.1.313 was distributed through Anthropic’s official account on Cursor. So far, neither Cursor nor Anthropic has explained how the attackers gained control of the account.

In search of cloud credentials

“It was a supply-chain compromise where the attacker gained access to the official distribution channel,” Phorian CTO and co-founder Luke Roberts told Ars. “The malicious version 2.1.313 was posted to the official Anthropic account, effectively superseding 2.1.312. Extensions auto-update in Cursor by default, but users can configure this in settings.” Phorian has more details here.

items.title: Sam Altman Thinks Your PC Is Wasting Precious RAM
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
"Looks like OpenAI CEO Sam Altman wants to own all the computing resources and rent out terminals to the world as a way of propping up his business plan, now that debt-ridden AI companies are teetering on the edge," writes ancient Slashdot reader Gilmoure. Tom's Hardware reports: In an interview over beers with the YouTube channel Cheeky Pint, Altman said that local inference, and, by extension, people having DRAM in computers at home, is "quite terrible." When discussing local inference on home computers with open-source models, Altman discussed the assumption that people will be able to run local AI on their own computers, the ones they may already own or want to build.
 
Then he explained why that's a bad idea (at the 29-minute mark): "From a global allocation perspective, actually, it's quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world's limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer and being used 5% of the time," Altman said. "You want maximum utilization in the cloud if you're trying to deal with this very supply-constrained environment. And somehow many people's intuition is the opposite of that."
 
While OpenAI does have some open-source models, its primary business is in closed-source models that run in data centers, so he's really defending the company's business model. OpenAI isn't exactly threatened by some laptops and gaming rigs just yet, but local AI could mean people one day paying less for subscriptions to models like GPT-6 Luna if they have the power to run them at home. Altman's talk suggests that the company would prefer that more RAM go to OpenAI's data centers rather than home computers, which also sparks enthusiast fears of not being able to own your own hardware or software, but rather rent an agent and a computer in the cloud.

items.title: Thousands of 'Ghost Students' Use AI to Steal Millions In Student Loans, DOJ Says
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
The Justice Department has charged five people in a crackdown on "ghost student" fraud, in which scammers allegedly use stolen identities and AI to enroll fake students in colleges, complete coursework, and collect federal student loan funds. Ars Technica reports: In a press release Thursday, the Department of Justice said it had uncovered a large-scale scheme relying partly on AI. The DOJ seized more than $750,000 in cryptocurrency from "a network associated with Kenyan nationals" after data analysis helped flag likely fraudsters. Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the DOJ's National Fraud Enforcement Division credited new fraud-detection measures implemented by the Trump administration for the arrests. He said that "this is the first international seizure of its kind in Kenya," while warning fraudsters that the crackdown has only just begun.
 
[...] At a press conference, McDonald was joined by FBI and Department of Education officials to explain how the scheme works. It starts with bad actors purchasing personally identifiable information (PII) of Americans -- most frequently targeting high school graduates who never attended college and went straight into the workforce. Once they have that sensitive data, they fill out the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA) while seeking to enroll in universities and community colleges. If accepted, student aid is distributed first to schools to cover tuition and fees, but any leftover money is deposited into bank accounts controlled by the fraudsters. Dozens of Americans have opened bank accounts to act as money mules for fraudsters, the DOJ said.
 
To keep money flowing, bad actors use AI to fill out applications, complete coursework, and even make it appear that a student is attending virtual sessions. "It looks like the ghost student is actually completing the class," McDonald said at the press conference. "Some even create the appearance of a fake student in an online classroom to trick schools into believing a real person is present. The goal is to keep the ghost student in school for as long as possible, semester after semester after semester." So far, the DOE has "identified over 830,000 potentially fraudulent federal student aid accounts created by using this PII of US citizens," officials said at the press conference. If all those accounts are ghost students, total losses come close to $130 million, the DOJ said.

Skills like coding scares a lot of people. The media has made it seem like writing computer code is a genius-level activity, as weird symbols race across the screen and techno music blares in the background.But the truth is that, coding is actually pretty easy.I’m not saying this to dismiss the work of brilliant programmers. A skill can simultaneously be fairly easy to get the basics in, while also being really difficult to master. Everyone learns to write, few people learn to write well. There’s no contradiction, therefore, in saying that basic literacy is an “easy” skill to acquire (in that the vast majority of us are able to do it), without dismissing the efforts of talented writers.Nor am I saying this to mock people who are trying to learn programming and find it frustrating.Rather, I say coding is easy because I believe that almost all people, even if they don’t see themselves as particularly smart, have the ability to learn to write simple programs. That they don’t is mostly due to some structural barriers than any intrinsic difficulty with the skill itself.My Experience CodingI started learning how to write code since I was 14. I’ve read a couple of O’Rielly books on programming, took even free courses on Coursera and Udemy. Watch thousands of hours on programming related videos on YouTube. I remember even working through the content of a Computer Science Degree online (which is totally unnecessary if you want to learn to code,by the way).If you take a closer look, in some ways... my background may seem to disqualify me about making statements on the ease of coding. However, I can say without a single doubt, that subjects like Accounting, Physics, Engineering and even Law are more difficult than programming.Most math you learn in high-school is more difficult too, believe it; although you usually get wayyyyy more practice with algebra than writing code, which leads to a misperception as to which is more difficult.Why Coding Feels HardLearning to code is hard for a couple reasons:Installing new languages can be super frustrating. This is the first activity for a wanna-be programmer. This can create the misperception that programming is really hard because newbies extrapolate the difficulty of getting set up to how it weill be every moment after.Also, there are waayyyyyyyy too many languages, frameworks tools, libraries and plug-ins. Starting programming is super overwhelming because there are a stadezillion things to learn and you have no idea where to start.The first moments of programming are the hardest. Getting set up is annoyingly difficult and often requires learning a new way of working with computers even before you write a single line of code.Consider the instructions for installing most languages:“Open the terminal or command prompt. Type in a case-sensitive exact set of instructions to download and install the language. Use GitHub. Homebrew. Versions matter too. Are you running 32 or 64 bit? ‘Cause if you’re not sure it will crash with a cryptic error message and you’ll feel like an idiot.”These tools are learnable, like everything else, but they reinforce the impression given by the media that coding is mostly using elite tools with weird, unfriendly user interfaces. When people see coding they imagine parsing the green-streaming letters on computer screens like the movie, The Matrix; whereas the truth is a lot more like following a recipe along step-by-step.How Do You Get Over the Initial Difficulties?There’s a few ways you can do this. My favorite is to just go to the language or technology official documentation, that will tell you exactly how to set up step-by-step.Alternatively, you can dive into internet tutorials (why do you think platforms like YouTube, Quora exists?), but recognize that sometimes they are aimed at already-proficient programmers, who know what OOP and GitHub are, and are fluent with writing commands into Terminal.If you get one of these, you can try to follow it, but don’t feel bad if you screw it up. It’s frustrating and it doesn’t mean all coding will be like this.Another option is to avoid setup at all. Just use some coding tutorial website that teach you to code without needing any installation. I like this too, but sometimes you can’t actually build the thing you want to build with these apps. However, if you hate the setup, that’s where I’d start.Most important, however, is to remember that I told you this. When you try to learn to code, it will be frustrating to get set up, and just accept that this is a small price to pay. Soon it will be easier and you’ll do stuff that is cool. Don’t feel dumb because you get stuck here, I still do and I’ve been writing code for years.What Language/Framework/Library Should I Start With?This seems like a good question to ask, but, I’d argue, it’s actually the wrong way to think about learning programming.First, despite the fact that programmers often boast about how many languages they know, recognize that most languages are only superficially different. Yes, I know all about language design, so don’t tell me about the importance of scripting versus compiling, or whether a language is strongly or weakly typed. Those things matter, but they’re details.The basics of nearly all languages and tools are the same. Variables. Loops. Functions. Pointers. Data Types. OOP. Modules. These concepts exist in almost all programming languages. If you pick a mainstream language, you’ll learn these in mostly the same way, so it doesn’t matter if you pick Python, JavaScript, C++, Java or even PHP.The place languages do matter is what you want to use them for.Want to write iPhone apps? Swift or Objective C are the languages of choice. Need to create web pages? JavaScript is going to come in handy. Yes, you can use almost any language for any task if you tinker with it and get the right plug-ins. However, some languages are easier to get started with certain types of projects than others.Therefore, the first question to ask is not: which language should I learn, but, which project should I start with?What Should Be Your First Project?I recommend starting your programming adventure, even before you write a single line of code, with a decision about a concrete programming project you’d like to create.This serves a couple purposes:It narrows down the language/framework choices considerably. Once you know you’re building a website, you’re already leaning towards tools that were designed with that goal in mind.Everything you learn is connected to a destination. Transfer of learning is notoriously difficult. Learning directly by building, works better than learning something and just hoping it will help you later.You can work on something you think is cool. If you think it would be cool to make an interactive website, do that. If you’d prefer a game, do that. If you’d prefer to automate some tedious work, do that instead. Do what you feel is cool and you’ll be motivated to stick to it.In general, smaller is better when it comes to projects. Deciding to start with making the next Google is ambitious, but probably will get you stuck in the weeds before you make much progress.If your true ambitious are huge, it’s often best to work on a toy project first. Many experienced programmers still do this when they are entering a new territory of programming. Toy projects take the essential ideas of programming, but turn it into something you can do in a few days or weeks, instead of years.Examples of good projects include:A basic terminal text-adventure game. No graphics, but still requires learning concepts like loops, variables, input-output processing.A simple website. Start with just displaying a static page. Maybe add in comments, users, photos or interactive elements as you learn more.A simple app. What’s something dead-simple you’d like to have on your phone? It can be stupid to start, don’t worry.A script for automating a tedious task.In general, programs are easier when they involve no multimedia content (websites are a bit of an exception), so if you’re making a game, for instance, a text game tends to be easier than one with graphics, if only because making all the graphics can take time.Similarly, different core activities have different difficulties. Arithmetic and simple calculations done repeatedly are easiest. Processing text for exact patterns is a bit harder. Processing text for vague patterns is harder still. Processing, speech, photos and video is even harder.If you do end up picking an initial project that turns out to be super difficult, it’s okay to scale back. “Make an application that calculates my mortgage payments” is much, much easier than “Make an application that can tell you what someone’s hairstyle is from a photo.” It’s often not obvious that this is the case in the beginning, so don’t worry if you accidentally pick a “hard” problem to start with, you can adjust it later to something easier.Which Resources Should You Use?Once you’ve picked a project, the next step is to get some resources to help. This is a step many people worry over endlessly, but like the language choice, it’s a lot less important (and depends more on your goals) than you think.I won’t list specific resources, because there are so many good ones that my suggestions are going to leave out some of the best. Instead, here’s three strategies for finding good resources:Get a book that teaches you the language + project you want. There should be a computer section in your city’s bookstore or library, you can just pick any of those. I personally like O’Reilly (they publish the best software development books), but there are lots of good ones. (If you haven’t figured out which language yet, just DuckDuckGo your type of project and look for suggestions.) I read the Self-taught programmer by Cory Altoff, the first time I wanted to learn Python.Attend a MOOC. Coursera, edX, MIT, Harvard, FreeCodeCamp and others all teach computer programming online. Once again, the thing that matters most isn’t the exact class, but whether it teaches the language/project domain you care about.Stressing over which book or course to pick is the wrong thing to worry about. The main thing to do is to use the book or course to learn enough to start tinkering on your project, not to master programming on its own. Starting your project before your ready is definitely the way you should feel about it.Do What Real Programmers Do and Ask DuckDuckGo/StackOverflow/GoogleOnce you actually get started writing code, you’re going to encounter many, many situations where you either don’t know how to do something, or you learned how to do it before and you’ve forgotten.In these situations, you should do what real programmers do: ask DuckDuckGo/Google/StackOverflow. This isn’t a shameful activity, but a part of real programming. I’ve been coding for years, but I always forget silly syntactical things and so I find myself duckduckgoing regular expressions over and over again. It’s not bad, it’s just part of the process.Once you’ve gotten yourself installed, you’ve learned a bit with your book to know the basics and have started working on your first project, you’ll learn the rest by googling and adding to your library of programming knowledge. Computer science theories, detailed understandings of the language you’re working with or advanced design patterns can wait until you’ve finished a few real projects and feel like you can code something.Notice #1: Don’t Copy-and-PasteA first piece of advice when it comes to this step is to never copy-and-paste. Copy-and-pasting is bad because you don’t try to understand the code you’re copying. If you have to transcribe, in contrast, you naturally ask yourself, “why this? why not something else?” Even if you don’t have a great answer immediately, typing things for yourself will open your mind up to the answer whereas copy-and-pasting shuts down thinking.Notice #2: Try it Yourself Before Looking for a SolutionA second piece of advice is to always try to solve something yourself before looking up how someone else does it. Most problems have many, many ways they can be solved. The challenge is that expert programmers often know a particularly concise, clever way, but that often isn’t the “obvious” way.This can lead to a trap where you see a clever solution that employs tricky syntax, think that there was no way you would have guessed that solution, and believe you couldn’t have solved it on your own. That’s usually not true, yet it’s an unfortunate side effect of looking up solutions before trying to find your own.Summary of AdvThisisting up is frustrating.

items.title: The Night He Came Home
items.author: Renan Botasse
items.content:
My name is Renan. I lived in Colatina, Brazil.

When I was a kid, Halloween did not exist on my street. October arrived hot, with the smell of the Rio Doce in the air and the late afternoon taking its time to go dark. There was no candy at the door, no costumes lined up on the sidewalk. There was, instead, the house we crossed faster, the one someone swore had a story. There were the adults’ warnings: don’t talk to strangers; don’t take long coming back; say where you are. Above all, there was the idea that something could cross the short distance between the gate and the corner and never return a child.

In Colatina, “witch” was not a costume imported from an American calendar. It was a word that dropped the volume of a conversation. I still did not know what that meant for real. I only knew that terror did not need a mask to work.

Years later, in a dark room, small TV, volume low so the house would not wake up, I reached , John Carpenter’s 1978 film, for the first time. I don’t remember if it was October. I remember the silence after the final credit. I remember thinking that film, shot in a suburb I had never seen, spoke to a fear I already knew: the quiet street, the half-open door, the “why” that never comes. It felt closer to real dread than any story where the monster explains the monster.

Maybe no one can fully explain what makes so effective. The most we can do, today, is try to understand a few facts.

In cinema, Halloween always existed. In American life, too: candy, costumes, the “haunted house” down the street. In Carpenter’s film, the date is not decoration. It is the thesis.

The story begins in 1963, on a Halloween night in Haddonfield. A six-year-old boy kills his own sister. Fifteen years later, in 1978, he escapes a psychiatric institution and returns to town. The film does not invent the slasher, but it organizes the genre with an almost cruel clarity: quiet suburb, teenage girl alone, heavy breathing offscreen, and a man, or what is left of a man, reduced to a silhouette.

Carpenter and Debra Hill wrote the screenplay in about ten days. The producers had come to him with the idea of a killer who hunted babysitters. There were rumors the original title would be ; Yablans, one of the producers, denied it. The film was always going to take place on Halloween. Carpenter liked that. It seemed too obvious, and for that very reason, no one had fully embraced the date until then.

Haddonfield, Illinois, is fiction. The name came from Debra Hill’s hometown in New Jersey. The county on the police badge points to Bowling Green, where Carpenter grew up. Laurie Strode carries the name of an old girlfriend of the director. Michael Myers, that of a British producer. Tommy Doyle and Dr. Samuel Loomis are Hitchcock echoes: and . Jamie Lee Curtis, in her first film, was the daughter of Janet Leigh. American cinema loves those invisible threads. Carpenter did too.

The budget was small, somewhere around $325,000. Donald Pleasence, as Loomis, made $20,000. Jamie Lee Curtis, $8,000. Nick Castle, under the mask, $25 a day. The mask came from a costume shop: a William Shatner face, Captain Kirk, bought for less than two dollars, painted white, the eyes widened. The actors’ own clothes, cars rented from a local dealer, dead leaves reused from scene to scene. Shot in spring, in California, with palm trees hidden in the frame and license plates kept out of the way to fake the Midwest. Robert Englund, years before Freddy Krueger, helped scatter leaves to manufacture autumn.

The film made tens of millions. But the number matters less than the feeling it left behind: that evil could live in the empty house at the end of the street, the one every child knows, even without knowing the name of whoever died inside.

In real life, after an atrocity, the first question is usually the same: why?

The human brain does not tolerate emptiness well. It wants motive, biography, trauma, a bank account, revenge. It wants to turn the absurd into an algorithm. refuses that comfort.

Michael Myers, in the credits, appears as . He is not a character in the classic sense. He is a presence. Loomis insists on calling him “it,” not “he.” Evil. A force. Something you watch, fear, try to lock away, and that still crosses the night.

There are readings. Michael saw sex too young and could not understand it. Laurie would remind him of Judith, the sister. Tommy, beside her when she drops the key at the Myers house, would be about the age Michael was in 1963. The killings would follow a ritual pattern: bedsheets, an improvised shrine, a body arranged like a scene. All of that may be true. None of it is stated in the 1978 film with the authority of a caption.

That is where the film parts ways with so many of its successors. has territory and revenge. A Nightmare on Elm Street has collective guilt. Michael, in the first film, has absence. The mask does not only hide the face: it hides intent. Without expression, we do not know if he enjoys it, if he hates, if he feels nothing at all. Without a “why,” the “what” gets worse.

The sequels tried to fill the hole: siblings, curses, supernatural answers. Some of those solutions land. None, to my mind, beats the question left open. Explaining Michael is domesticating him. And domestic fear, the residential street, the half-open door, loses its force when it becomes a manual.

Carpenter and Hill also said later that Laurie’s survival was not a prize for virginity, a Freudian reading critics fastened on too quickly. Laurie survives because she pays attention. Because she is not distracted. Because, in the end, she fights back. The rest is couch theory.

How you film what has no name

The film opens with a long shot, almost voyeuristic, through the killer’s eyes. The inspiration points back to Orson Welles’s : a take that forces us to follow the crime as accomplices. At the end, the mask comes off and we see a child. The shock is not only the murder. It is the age.

The score, by Carpenter himself, in time signatures his father taught him, does half the work. The story goes that an executive watched the film without the music and did not find it scary. With the score, he changed his mind. A few notes. Enough.

Dean Cundey, the cinematographer, and the early use of the Panaglide give the film that restless glide: the camera follows, breathes, does not cut to spare us. The spaces keep getting smaller: street, house, room, closet. At the start, there is a world. By the end, there is creaking wood and almost nowhere left to run.

There is also the dry humor of cheap production turning into style. Precarious lighting that swallows detail. The asylum car appearing in the background while Laurie talks. Myers driving with the mask dead straight, an image at once terrifying and absurd. Annie in the laundry room, and us, who saw what she did not, begging in our heads: don’t go that way.

The safe suburb, the cliché the film helped crystallize, works because Carpenter films observation first, not the slaughter. Michael is a stalker before he is an executioner. The paranoia builds in the corner of the frame. When the violence arrives, it is already late: the fear came first.

Samhain, the haunted house, and what remains

Behind the scenes, people talk about Samhain, the Celtic festival when the dead cross the veil. They talk about evil that cannot be killed. They talk about the Myers house as the haunted house every town invents for itself. Carpenter wanted that universal recognition: the place you walk past faster, without admitting why.

Loomis describes Michael with the coldness of someone who spent fifteen years staring into an abyss that stared back. Pleasence took the role after Cushing and Christopher Lee turned it down. Lee would later call that refusal the biggest mistake of his career. In a few days of shooting, a friendship with Carpenter was born that would lead to other films.

In the end, Loomis shoots. Six times. In the heart. Michael falls. Then he is gone. The film does not celebrate victory. It offers a montage of empty places, the house, the street, the night, with the breathing still on top. He could be anywhere. Including, the cut suggests, nowhere.

It is an honest ending. Because the fear stages is not the fear of a monster with clear rules. It is the fear of explanatory emptiness. The same emptiness that makes a small inland town invent witches when it cannot stand being without a cause. The same one that makes an adult, decades later, remember a street in Colatina at dusk and feel the stomach close, not because of a movie ghost, but because of the old certainty that the dark, there, never needed subtitles.

A note, if a note belongs

I am not saying a 1978 horror film and the fear of growing up in a small town are the same thing. They are not. One is an artifact. The other is memory. But both, each in its way, deal with the same human difficulty: what to do when the “why” does not come.

runs a little over ninety minutes and costs almost nothing on paper. It still scares because it respects the viewer’s intelligence, and because it respects the terror of not knowing. Simplicity. Ambiguity. One night. One street. A white shape walking without hurry.

Halloween, on the calendar, is make-believe. In Carpenter’s film, it is a warning.

This is the night he came home.

And the question that remains, the only one the film refuses to kill along with the victims, is not whether Michael Myers is a man, a demon, or a cheap-production accident.

It is another, older, and far less comfortable:

If evil needs no reason to cross your street… anyone can be its victim, without warning, without sense, again, without motive.

items.title: GM Reaches $220 Million Settlement Over Selling Drivers' Private Data
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from TechCrunch: General Motors will pay $220 million to 36 states to settle allegations that it illegally sold private driving behavior and location information to data brokers. As part of the settlement, GM must get drivers' express consent before it collects or shares their driving and location data -- terms that are in line with separate agreements it previously reached with California and the Federal Trade Commission (FTC). This settlement does contain a new requirement that GM must have a third party assess the automaker's compliance with the privacy program it has put in place.
 
The agreement announced Thursday settles a lawsuit brought by a coalition of attorneys general from 36 states that alleged GM had sold the information to data brokers, which in turn then sold it to insurance providers. "This agreement addresses Smart Driver, a product we ended in 2024, and reinforces steps we've taken to strengthen our privacy practices," GM said in an emailed statement. "Safer, more helpful and personalized experiences are enabled by connected vehicle data, and GM is committed to being clear about what information is used, how it's protected, and the choices customers have about what they share."
 
The settlement comes more than two years after a New York Times report showed how GM and OnStar collected, used, and sold drivers' precise geolocation data and driving behavior to third parties, including data brokers LexisNexis and Verisk. The data was collected through GM's Smart Driver program, a free feature contained within its connected car apps that tracked and rated driving behaviors and seat belt use. Data brokers sold this information to insurance providers, which could affect customers' rates, the NYT reported at the time.
